accroche: In 1620, Francis Bacon lists the traps the mind sets for itself, before any experiment has even begun.
contenu_vulgarise:
A stick dipped in water looks broken. Two parallel rails seem to converge at the horizon. In both cases, the eyes do not lie about what they see, yet the judgment that draws a conclusion about the world from them can still be wrong. Francis Bacon, Lord Chancellor of England who fell in disgrace over corruption charges in 1621, publishes the year before a book that claims to catalogue these traps in full: the *Novum Organum* (“New Instrument”), 1620.

## Four classes of idols

Bacon distinguishes four classes of idols there, in the sense of illusions rather than objects of worship, which systematically distort judgment before any experiment even takes place.

The idols of the tribe stem from human nature itself: “the human understanding is like a false mirror, which, receiving rays irregularly, distorts and discolours the nature of things by mingling its own nature with it” (aphorism 41). The idols of the cave are specific to each individual: one's education, readings, and admired authorities make up a cave one never fully leaves. The idols of the marketplace arise from language: words are fixed according to the understanding of ordinary people, not according to the nature of things, and once fixed they impose their own divisions on thought. The idols of the theatre, finally, come from received philosophical systems: Bacon places there Aristotelianism, an empiricism that generalizes too quickly from a handful of experiments, and superstition, three stage-plays that give the illusion of a coherent world without ever having been verified.

## What this shifts

Bacon does not propose to eliminate these idols: he holds them to be unavoidable, lodged in the mind like dust in the air. His move lies elsewhere, in naming precisely four distinct sources of error, so that a researcher faced with any hasty conclusion can ask which one it stems from. Two centuries before Claude Bernard mocked the “average urine” of the train station, Bacon already had a word for that very bias: the idol of the tribe, which takes the measure of one individual for the measure of the universe. The whole project of the *Novum Organum* draws a method from this, set out in aphorism 70: to seek “experiments of light, not experiments of fruit,” experiments that illuminate a principle rather than ones that merely produce a pleasing result. A science that does not first spot its own traps, Bacon suggests, only reproduces them with better instruments.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon say that the human understanding is a false mirror?
choix: Because the senses always deceive us about the real shape of objects
Because judgment mixes its own nature into what it perceives, instead of reflecting it faithfully
Because light physically distorts when passing through the human eye
Because only philosophers of Antiquity suffered from this flaw
quiz.explication: Bacon does not say the senses lie about the shape of objects, that is not an optical flaw, nor does he hold the trait to be unique to Antiquity, he treats it as universal: the idol of the tribe is that human judgment mixes its own nature into what it perceives, like a mirror that distorts as it reflects.
